[[Legion of Honour]] (France) | relatives = | image_size = 250 | monarch = [[Queen Victoria|Victoria]] | resting_place = [[St. Paul's Cathedral]], [[London]] | prime_minister = [[Robert Gascoyne-Cecil, 3rd Marquess of Salisbury|Marquess of Salisbury]] | parents = | spouse = {{marriage|Louisa Erskine|1867}} | children = [[Frances Garnet Wolseley, 2nd Viscountess Wolseley]] }} [[Field marshal (United Kingdom)|Field Marshal]] '''Garnet Joseph Wolseley, 1st Viscount Wolseley''' (4 June 1833{{snd}}25 March 1913) was an [[Anglo-Irish]] officer in the [[British Army]]. He became one of the most influential British generals after a series of victories in Canada, West Africa and Egypt, followed by a central role in modernizing the British Army in promoting efficiency. Wolseley is considered to be one of the most prominent and decorated war heroes of the [[British Empire]] during the era of [[New Imperialism]]. He served in Burma, the [[Crimean War]], the [[Indian Mutiny]], China, Canada and widely throughout Africa—including his [[Anglo-Ashanti wars|Ashanti]] campaign (1873–1874) and the [[Nile Expedition]] against [[Mahdist War|Mahdist]] Sudan in 1884–85. Wolseley served as [[Commander-in-Chief of the Forces]] from 1895 to 1900. His reputation for efficiency led to the late 19th century English phrase "everything's all Sir Garnet", meaning, "All is in order."{{sfn|Farmer|Henley|1903|p=215}} ==Early life and education == Lord Wolseley was born into a prominent [[Anglo-Irish people|Anglo-Irish]] family in [[Dublin]], the eldest son of [[Major (British Army)|Major]] Garnet Joseph Wolseley of the [[King's Own Scottish Borderers]] ([[25th Foot]]) and Frances Anne Wolseley (''née'' Smith). The Wolseleys were an ancient landed family in [[Wolseley, Staffordshire]], whose roots can be traced back a thousand years.{{cite newspaper The Times |title=Death of Lord Wolseley |page=7 |date=26 March 1913 }} Wolseley was born at Golden Bridge House, the seat of his mother's family. His paternal grandfather was Rev. William Wolseley, Rector of [[Tullycorbet]], and the third son of [[Sir Richard Wolseley, 1st Baronet]], who sat in the [[Irish House of Commons]] for [[Carlow (Parliament of Ireland constituency)|Carlow]].{{cite book|title=Burke's Genealogical and Heraldic History of the Peerage, Baronetage and Knightage|year=1885|publisher=Burke's Peerage Limited|page=1425|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6u8_AQAAMAAJ&pg=PA1425|access-date=28 June 2017}} The family seat was Mount Wolseley in [[County Carlow]].{{cite book|title=Complete Baronetage: Great Britain and Ireland, 1707–1800, and Jacobite, 1688–1788|year=1906|publisher=W. Pollard & Company, Limited|pages=356–357|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gMpKAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA356}} He had four younger sisters and two younger brothers, [[Frederick Wolseley]] (1837–1899) and [[George Wolseley|Sir George Wolseley]] (1839–1921). Wolseley's father died in 1840 at age 62, leaving his widow and seven children to struggle on his Army pension. Unlike other boys in his class, Wolseley was not sent to England to attend [[Harrow School|Harrow]] or [[Eton College|Eton]], but was instead educated at a local school in Dublin. There, he enjoyed military history and the Latin classics, and excelled at mathematics, history, drawing, reading, and sports.{{Cite book |last=Kochanski |first=Halik |url= |title=Sir Garnet Wolseley: Victorian Hero |date=1 January 1999 |publisher=A&C Black |isbn=978-1-85285-188-0 |pages=2 |language=en}}{{Cite book |last=Manning |first=Stephen |url= |title=Sir Garnet Wolseley: Soldier of Empire |date=1 February 2024 |publisher=Pen and Sword Military |isbn=978-1-3990-7247-2 |pages=3 |language=en}} However, the family circumstance forced Wolseley to leave school at age 14, when he found work in a [[Surveying|surveyor]]'s office, which helped him bring in a salary and continue studying mathematics and geography.{{cite web|title=Field Marshal Garnet Joseph Wolseley, 1st Viscount Wolseley, KP, GCB, OM, GCMG, VD, PC.|url=http://www.irishmasonichistory.com/field-marshal-garnet-joseph-wolseley-1st-viscount-wolseley-kp-gcb-om-gcmg-vd-pc.html|website=Irish Masonic History and the Jewels of Irish Freemasonry|access-date=28 June 2017}}{{cite ODNB|id=36995|title=Garnet Wolseley, 1st Viscount Wolseley}} The methodical nature of the job, with its need for attention to detail, would prove to serve him well in his future army career. == Early military career == Wolseley first considered a career in the church, but his financial situation meant that he would have needed a wealthy patron to support such an endeavour. Instead he sought a [[Officer (armed forces)|commission]] in the Army. Unable to afford [[Royal Military College, Sandhurst|Sandhurst]] or [[Sale of commissions|buying a commission]], Wolseley wrote to his fellow Dubliner, [[Field Marshal (United Kingdom)|Field Marshal]] [[Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington|The 1st Duke of Wellington]], for assistance. Wellington, then the [[Commander-in-Chief of the Forces]], promised to assist him when he turned 16. However, Wellington apparently overlooked him and did not respond to another letter sent when he was 17. Wolseley unsuccessfully appealed to his secretary, [[FitzRoy Somerset, 1st Baron Raglan|Lord Fitzroy Somerset]]. The British Army was then recovering from significant casualties in the latest [[Xhosa Wars|war in South Africa]], and Wolseley wrote to Somerset, "I shall be prepared to start at the shortest notice, should your Lordship be pleased to appoint me to a regiment now at the seat of war." His mother then wrote to the Duke to appeal his case, and on 12 March 1852, the 18-year-old Wolseley was [[Gazette#Gazette as a verb|gazetted]] as an [[ensign (rank)|ensign]] in the [[Suffolk Regiment|12th Foot]],{{London Gazette|issue=21300|page=768|date=12 March 1852}} in recognition of his father's service. Just a month after he joined the [[Suffolk Regiment|12th Foot]], Wolseley transferred to the [[80th Regiment of Foot (Staffordshire Volunteers)|80th Foot]] on 13 April 1852,{{London Gazette|issue=21309|page=1058|date=13 April 1852|nolink=y}} with whom he served in the [[Second Anglo-Burmese War]].{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=311}} He was severely wounded when he was shot in the left thigh with a [[jingal]] bullet on 19 March 1853 in the attack on [[Donabyu]],{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=311}} and was [[mentioned in despatches]]. Promoted to [[lieutenant]] on 16 May 1853 and invalided home, Wolseley transferred to the [[84th (York and Lancaster) Regiment of Foot|84th Regiment of Foot]] on 27 January 1854,{{London Gazette|issue=21515|page=232|date=27 January 1854|nolink=y}} and then to the [[90th Regiment of Foot (Perthshire Volunteers)|90th Light Infantry]],{{London Gazette|issue=21526|page=642|date=24 February 1854|nolink=y}} at that time stationed in [[Dublin]], on 24 February 1854.{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=311}} He was promoted to [[Captain (British Army and Royal Marines)|captain]] on 29 December 1854.{{London Gazette|issue=21645|page=4259|date=29 December 1854|nolink=y}} ==Crimea== Wolseley accompanied the regiment to [[Crimean War|the Crimea]], and landed at [[Balaklava]] in December 1854. He was selected to be an assistant [[Military engineer|engineer]], and attached to the [[Royal Engineers]] during the [[Crimean War#Siege of Sevastopol|Siege of Sevastopol]]. Wolseley served throughout the siege, where he was wounded at "the Quarries" on 7 June 1855, and again in the trenches on 30 August 1855, losing an eye.{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=311}} After the fall of [[Sevastopol]], Wolseley was employed on the [[quartermaster-general]]'s staff, assisting in the embarkation of the troops and supplies, and was one of the last British soldiers to leave the Crimea in July 1856.{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=311}} For his services he was twice mentioned in despatches, received the war medal with clasp, the 5th class of the French ''[[Légion d'honneur]]''{{London Gazette|issue=21909|page=2699|date=4 August 1856|nolink=y}} and the 5th class of the Turkish [[Order of the Medjidie]].{{cite EB1911|wstitle=Wolseley, Garnet Joseph Wolseley, Viscount|volume=28|pages=777–778}}{{London Gazette|issue=22107|page=1264|date=2 March 1858|nolink=y}} Six months after joining the [[90th Foot]] at [[Aldershot]], he went with it in March 1857 to join the troops being despatched for the [[Second Opium War]].{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=311}} Wolseley was embarked in the transport ''Transit'', which wrecked in the [[Bangka Strait|Strait of Banka]]. The troops were all saved, but with only their personal arms and minimal ammunition. They were taken to [[Singapore]], and from there dispatched to [[Calcutta]] on account of the [[Indian Mutiny]].{{cite web|url=http://www.timmonet.co.uk/html/body_wolseley.htm|title=A Victorian Army Hero|publisher=Timmonet|access-date=26 February 2012}} ==Indian Rebellion of 1857== [[File:Felice Beato (British, born Italy - (Lieutenant-Colonel Wolsely, V.C.) - Google Art Project.jpg|thumb|left|Lieutenant-Colonel Wolseley in India, by [[Felice Beato]], 1858–1859]] Wolseley distinguished himself at the [[relief of Lucknow]] under Sir [[Colin Campbell, 1st Baron Clyde|Colin Campbell]] in November 1857, and in the defence of the [[Alambagh]] position under [[Sir James Outram, 1st Baronet|Outram]],{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=311}} taking part in the actions of 22 December 1857, of 12 January 1858 and 16 January 1858, and also in the repulse of the grand attack of 21 February 1858. That March, he served at the final [[siege of Lucknow|siege]] and capture of Lucknow. He was then appointed deputy-assistant quartermaster-general on the staff of Sir [[Hope Grant]]'s [[Oudh]] division, and was engaged in all of the operations of the campaign, including the actions of [[Bari, India|Bari]], [[Purnia division#Sarsi|Sarsi]], [[Kanpur|Nawabganj]], the capture of [[Faizabad]], the passage of the [[Gumti]] and the action of [[Sultanpur, Uttar Pradesh|Sultanpur]]. In the autumn and winter of 1858–59 he took part in the [[Lalganj, Uttar Pradesh|Baiswara]], trans-[[Gogra]] and trans-[[West Rapti River|Rapti]] campaigns ending with the complete suppression of the [[rebellion]]. For his services he was frequently mentioned in dispatches, and having received the [[Indian Mutiny Medal|Mutiny medal]] and clasp, he was promoted to brevet [[Major (rank)|major]] on 24 March 1858{{London Gazette|issue=22117|page=1571|date=24 March 1858|nolink=y}} and to brevet [[lieutenant-colonel]] on 26 April 1859.{{London Gazette|issue=22255|page=1727|date=26 April 1859|nolink=y}} During the rebellion, Wolseley displayed strong views towards native peoples, referring to them as "beastly [[nigger]]s", and remarking that the [[sepoys]] had "barrels and barrels of the filth which flows in these niggers' veins".{{cite book |last=Hibbert |first=Christopher |title=The Great Mutiny: India 1857 |date=1978 |publisher=Viking Press |isbn=978-0-670-34983-8 |page=254 |author-link=Christopher Hibbert}} Wolseley continued to serve on Sir Hope Grant's staff in Oudh, and when Grant was nominated to the [[Chain of command|command]] of the British troops in the [[Second Opium War|Anglo-French expedition to China]] of 1860,{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=311}} accompanied him as the deputy-assistant quartermaster-general. He was present at the action at [[Sin Ho District|Sin-ho]], the capture of [[Tanggu District|Tang-ku]], the storming of the [[Taku Forts]],{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=311}} the Occupation of [[Tianjin|Tientsin]], the Battle of [[Xilin County|Pa-to-cheau]] and the entry into [[Peking]] (during which the destruction of the [[Chinese people|Chinese]] [[Chinese Emperor|Imperial]] [[Old Summer Palace]] was begun).{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=311}} He assisted in the re-embarkation of the troops before the winter set in. He was Mentioned, yet again, in Dispatches, and for his services received the medal and two clasps. On his return home he published the ''Narrative of the War with China'' in 1860.{{sfn|Wolseley|1862}} He was given the substantive rank of [[Major (rank)|major]] on 15 February 1861.{{London Gazette|issue=22480|page=654|date=15 February 1861|nolink=y}} ==American Civil War and Canadian service== [[File:Viscount Garnet Joseph Wolseley.jpeg|thumb|right|Field Marshal Viscount Wolseley]] After the outbreak of the [[American Civil War]], Wolseley was one of the special service officers sent to the [[Province of Canada]] in November 1861, in connection with the [[Trent Affair|''Trent'' incident]]. In 1862, shortly after the [[Battle of Antietam]], Wolseley took leave from his military duties and went to investigate the [[American Civil War]]. He befriended [[Confederate States of America|Southern]] sympathizers in [[Maryland]], who found him passage into [[Virginia]] with a [[blockade runner]] across the [[Potomac River]]. There he met Generals [[Robert E. Lee]], [[James Longstreet]] and [[Stonewall Jackson]].{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=311}} He also provided an analysis of Lieutenant General [[Nathan Bedford Forrest]]. The ''[[New Orleans Picayune]]'' (10 April 1892) published Wolseley's ten-page portrayal of Forrest, which condensed much of what was written about him by biographers of the time. This work appeared in the ''Journal of the Southern Historical Society'' in the same year, and is commonly cited today. Wolseley addressed Forrest's role at the [[Battle of Fort Pillow]] near [[Memphis, Tennessee]], in April 1864 in which [[African-American|black]] [[United States Colored Troops|USCT]] troops and [[White people|white]] officers were alleged by some to have been slaughtered after [[Fort Pillow, Tennessee|Fort Pillow]] had been conquered. Wolseley wrote, "I do not think that the fact that one-half of the small garrison of a place taken by assault was either killed or wounded evinced any very unusual bloodthirstiness on the part of the assailants."''United Service Magazine'', London, 1892, April and May issues Following the end of the Civil War in the United States, Wolseley returned to Canada, where he became a brevet [[Colonel (United Kingdom)|colonel]] on 5 June 1865{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=311}} and Assistant Quartermaster-General in Canada with effect from the same date.{{London Gazette|issue=22992|page=3579|date=18 July 1865|nolink=y}} He was actively employed the following year in the defence of Canada from [[Fenian raids]] launched from the United States. He was appointed Deputy Quartermaster-General in Canada on 1 October 1867.{{London Gazette|issue=23278|page=4045|date=19 July 1867|nolink=y}} In 1869 his ''Soldiers' Pocket Book for Field Service'' was published. In its pages Wolseley gave his opinion on the fitness of the officer corps of his time and other sensitive subjects. For that he was put on half-pay, according to one source.{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=312}}{{Cite book |last=Morris |first=Donald |title=Washing of the Spears |pages=239}} In 1870, he led the [[Wolseley Expedition|Red River Expedition]] against the [[Red River Rebellion|uprising]] in the [[North-West Territories]] (present-day [[Manitoba]]), establishing Canadian colonial sovereignty in the province.{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=312}} As part of the [[North-West Territories]], Manitoba formally entered [[Canadian Confederation]] in 1870 when the [[Hudson's Bay Company]] transferred its control of [[Rupert's Land]] to the government of the Dominion of Canada. However, British and Canadian authorities ignored the pre-existing [[Council of Assiniboia]] and botched negotiations with its [[Métis people (Canada)|Métis]] replacement, the provisional government headed by [[Louis Riel]], who sought to join Canada on their own terms.{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=312}} The expedition was made difficult by challenging terrain and a lack of easily navigable routes, Canada not yet having a transcontinental railway line. [[Fort Garry]] (now [[Winnipeg]]), the [[Capital (political)|capital]] of Manitoba, was separated from eastern Canada by the rocks and forests of the [[Canadian Shield]] region of [[northwestern Ontario]]. The easiest route to Fort Garry that did not pass through the United States was through a network of rivers and lakes extending for {{convert|600|mi|order=flip}} from [[Lake Superior]], rarely traversed by those who were not part of the [[fur trade]], and where a conventional army would struggle to obtain supplies.{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=312}} An end to the uprising was negotiated while Wolseley's force was en route, but in recognition of his achievements in successfully leading the expedition, Wolseley was made a [[Knight Commander of the Order of St Michael and St George]] on his return home to Britain on 22 December 1870,{{London Gazette|issue=23690|page=5873|date=23 December 1870|nolink=y}} and a [[Companion of the Order of the Bath]] on 13 March 1871.{{London Gazette|issue=23715|page=1378|date=14 March 1871|nolink=y}} ==Cardwell reforms== Appointed assistant [[adjutant-general]] at the [[War Office]] in 1871, he furthered the [[Cardwell reforms|Cardwell schemes of army reform]].{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=312}} The reforms met strong opposition from senior military figures led by the [[Prince George, Duke of Cambridge|Duke of Cambridge]], [[Commander-in-Chief of the Forces]].{{sfn|McElwee|1974|p=73}} At their heart was the intent to expand greatly the Army's latent strength by building reserves, both through introducing legislation for 'short service',{{sfn|Ensor|1936|p=16}} which allowed soldiers to serve the second part of their term on the reserve, and by bringing militia (i.e. non-regular) battalions into the new localised regimental structure. Resistance in the Army continued and, in a series of subsequent military posts, Wolseley fought publicly as well as inside the Army's structure to implement them, long after the legislation had passed and Cardwell had gone.{{sfn|Lehmann|1964|p=224}}{{sfn|Gregory|2006|p=103}} ==Ashanti== [[File:Garnet Joseph Wolseley, 1874.png|thumb|Wolseley in 1874, from the ''[[Illustrated London News]]'']] On 2 October 1873, Wolseley became Governor of [[Sierra Leone]] British West African Settlements, and the Governor of the Gold Coast. As Governor of both British Territories in West Africa he had charge over the Colonies of [[Gambia]], [[Gold Coast (British colony)|Gold Coast]] and Western, Eastern, and Northern [[Nigeria]], and in this role, commanded an expedition against the [[Ashanti Empire]]. Wolseley made all his arrangements at Gold Coast before the arrival of the troops in January 1874. At the [[Battle of Amoaful]] on 31 January, Wolseley's expedition defeated the numerically superior Chief Amankwatia's army in a four-hour battle, advancing through thick bush in [[infantry square|loose squares]]. After five days' fighting, ending with the [[Battle of Ordashu]], the British entered the capital [[Kumasi]], which they burned. Wolseley completed the campaign in two months,{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=312}} and re-embarked his troops for home before the unhealthy season began. This campaign made him a household name in Britain. He received the thanks of both houses of [[Parliament of England|Parliament]] and a grant of £25,000, was promoted to brevet [[major-general]] for distinguished service in the field on 1 April 1874,{{London Gazette|issue=24082|page=1924|date=31 March 1874|nolink=y}} received the medal and clasp, and was made [[Knight Grand Cross of the Order of St Michael and St George]] on 31 March 1874,{{London Gazette|issue=24083|page=1971|date=3 April 1874|nolink=y}} and a [[Knight Commander of the Order of the Bath]]. The [[freedom of the city]] of [[City of London|London]] was conferred upon him with a sword of honour, and he was made honorary DCL of [[University of Oxford|Oxford]] and LL.D of [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]] universities.{{cite web|url=https://dib.cambridge.org/viewFullScreen.do?filename=/app/dib/production/content/html/9780521633314_9110.htm|title=Wolseley, Garnet Joseph|publisher=Dictionary of Irish Biography|access-date=15 January 2021}} ==Service at home, and in Natal, Cyprus, and South Africa== On his return home he was appointed inspector-general of Auxiliary Forces with effect from 1 April 1874.{{London Gazette|issue=24085|page=2061|date=10 April 1874|nolink=y}} In his role with the Auxiliary Forces, he directed his efforts to building up adequate volunteer reserve forces. Finding himself opposed by the senior military, he wrote a strong memorandum and spoke of resigning when they tried to persuade him to withdraw it.{{sfn|Lehmann|1964|p=224}} He became a lifelong advocate of the volunteer reserves, later commenting that all military reforms since 1860 in the British Army had first been introduced by the volunteers.{{sfn|Gregory|2006|p=103}} Shortly after, in consequence of the indigenous unrest in [[Colony of Natal|Natal]], he was sent to that colony as governor and general-commanding on 24 February 1875.{{London Gazette|issue=24184|page=810|date=26 February 1875|nolink=y}} [[File:Portrait_of_Sir_Garnet_Wolseley_1876.jpg|thumb|Wolseley in 1876, from ''Men of Mark'']] Wolseley accepted a seat on the [[Council of India]] in November 1876 and was promoted to the substantive rank of [[major-general]] on 1 October 1877.{{London Gazette|issue=24508|page=5460|date=2 October 1877|nolink=y}} He was promoted to brevet [[lieutenant-general]] on 25 March 1878.{{London Gazette|issue=24574|page=2638|date=19 April 1878|nolink=y}} On 12 July 1878, he was appointed [[List of High Commissioners of the United Kingdom to Cyprus|the first High Commissioner to Cyprus]], a newly acquired possession.{{London Gazette|issue=24605|page=4154|date=16 July 1878|nolink=y}} In the following year, he was sent to South Africa to supersede [[Frederic Thesiger, 2nd Baron Chelmsford|Lord Chelmsford]] in command of the forces in the [[Zulu War]],{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=312}} and as governor of [[Colony of Natal|Natal]] and the [[South African Republic|Transvaal]] and the [[High Commissioner]] of [[Southern Africa]]. Wolseley with his 'Ashanti Ring' of adherents was sent to [[Durban]]. But on arrival in July, he found that the Zulu War was practically over.{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=312}} After effecting a temporary settlement, he went on to the Transvaal. While serving in South Africa, he was promoted to brevet [[Army general|general]] on 4 June 1879.{{London Gazette|issue=24730|page=3731|date=3 June 1879|nolink=y}} Having reorganized the administration there and reduced King [[Sekhukhune]] of the [[Bapedi]] to submission, he returned to London in May 1880. For his services in South Africa, he was awarded the [[South Africa Medal (1877)|South Africa Medal]] with clasp, and was advanced to [[Knight Grand Cross of the Order of the Bath]] on 19 June 1880.{{London Gazette|issue=24857|page=3587|date=22 June 1880|nolink=y}} Finally, as if to signify a meteoric rise in Imperial esteem, he was appointed [[Quartermaster-General to the Forces]] on 1 July 1880.{{London Gazette|issue=24838|page=2727|date=27 April 1880|nolink=y}} He found that there was still great resistance to the short service system and used his growing public persona to fight for the Cardwell reforms, especially on building up reserves, including making a speech at a banquet in Mansion house in which he commented: '...how an Army raised under the long service system totally disappeared in a few months under the walls of Sevastopol.'{{sfn|Lehmann|1964|p=224}} ==Egypt, the Nile Expedition and Commander-in-Chief== [[File:Garnet wolseley cartoon.png|thumb|left|1882 [[caricature]] from [[Punch (magazine)|Punch]]]] [[File:Queen Victoria's funeral procession.jpg|thumb|left|Queen Victoria's funeral procession]] [[File:Edward VIIs coronation procession London 9 August 1902.jpg|thumb|left|Edward VIIs coronation procession London 9 August 1902]] On 1 April 1882, Wolseley was appointed [[Adjutant-General to the Forces]],{{London Gazette|issue=25084|page=1131|date=14 March 1882|nolink=y}} and, in August of that year, given command of the British forces in Egypt under [[Khedive Tewfik]] to suppress the [[Urabi Revolt]].{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=313}} Having seized the [[Suez Canal]], he then disembarked his troops at [[Ismailia]] and, after a very short campaign, completely defeated [[Ahmed 'Urabi|Urabi Pasha]] at the [[Battle of Tel el-Kebir]], thereby suppressing yet another rebellion.{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=313}} For his services, he was promoted to the substantive rank of [[general (British Army)|general]] on 18 November{{London Gazette|issue=25169|page=5173|date=17 November 1882|nolink=y}} and raised to the [[Peerage of the United Kingdom|peerage]] as '''Baron Wolseley''', of [[Cairo]] and of [[Wolseley, Staffordshire|Wolseley]] in the County of Stafford. He also received the thanks of Parliament and [[Egypt Medal|the Egypt Medal]] with clasp;{{London Gazette|issue=25170|page=5195|date=21 November 1882|nolink=y}} the [[Order of Osmanieh]], First Class, as bestowed by the [[Khedive]];{{London Gazette|issue=25168|page=5106|date=17 November 1882|nolink=y}} and the more dubious accolade of a composition in his honour by [[poetaster]] [[William Topaz McGonagall]].{{cite web|url=http://www.mcgonagall-online.org.uk/gems/the-battle-of-tel-el-kebir|title=The Battle of Tel-el-Kebir|date=23 August 2011 |publisher=Mcgonagall|access-date=16 September 2015}} On 1 September 1884, Wolseley was again called away from his duties as adjutant-general, to command the [[Nile Expedition]] for the relief of [[Charles George Gordon|General Gordon]] and the besieged garrison at [[Khartoum]]. Wolseley's unusual strategy was to take an expedition by boat up the Nile and then to cross the desert to Khartoum, while the naval boats went on to Khartoum.{{London Gazette|issue=25394|page=4040|date=9 September 1884|nolink=y}} The expedition arrived too late; Khartoum had been taken, and Gordon was dead.{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=313}} In the spring of 1885, complications with [[Imperial Russia]] over the [[Panjdeh Incident]] occurred, and the withdrawal of that particular expedition followed. For his services there, he received two clasps to his Egyptian medal, the thanks of Parliament, and on 28 September 1885 was created '''Viscount Wolseley''', of Wolseley in the County of Stafford,{{London Gazette|issue=25514|page=4515|date=25 September 1885|nolink=y}}{{sfn|Cokayne|1898|p=195}} and a [[Knight of the Order of St Patrick]]. At the invitation of the [[Queen Victoria|Queen]], the Wolseley family moved from their former home at 6 [[Hill Street, London]] to the much grander [[Ranger's House]] in [[Greenwich]] in autumn 1888.{{sfn|James|2012|p=229}} Wolseley continued at the War Office as [[Adjutant-General to the Forces]] until 1890, when he became [[Commander-in-Chief, Ireland]].{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=313}} He was promoted to be a field marshal on 26 May 1894,{{London Gazette|issue=26516|page=3117|date=26 May 1894|nolink=y}} and appointed by the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] [[Her Majesty's Government|government]] to succeed the [[Prince George, Duke of Cambridge|Duke of Cambridge]] as [[Commander-in-Chief of the Forces]] on 1 November 1895.{{London Gazette|issue=26676|page=5923|date=1 November 1895|nolink=y}} This was the position to which his great experience in the field and his previous signal success at the War Office itself had fully entitled him, but it was increasingly irrelevant. Field Marshal Viscount Wolseley's powers in that office were, however, limited by a new [[Order in Council]], and after holding the appointment for over five years, he handed over the command-in-chief to his fellow field marshal, [[Frederick Roberts, 1st Earl Roberts|Earl Roberts]], on 3 January 1901.{{London Gazette|issue=27263|page=83|date=4 January 1901|nolink=y}} He had also suffered from a serious illness in 1897, from which he never fully recovered.{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=313}} The unexpectedly large force required for the initial phase of the [[Second Boer War]], was mainly furnished by means of the system of reserves Wolseley had originated. By drawing on regular reservists and volunteer reserves, Britain was able to assemble the largest army it had ever deployed abroad.{{cite web|url=https://www.familyhistory.co.uk/the-boer-war/|title=The Boer War|publisher=Family History|access-date=15 January 2021}} Nevertheless, the new conditions at the War Office were not to his liking. The fiasco now called [[Black Week]] culminated in his dismissal over Christmastide 1900. Upon being released from responsibilities he brought the whole subject before the [[House of Lords]] in a speech.{{cite web|url=https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/lords/1901/mar/04/war-office-administration-duties-of#S4V0090P0_19010304_HOL_56|title=War Office Administration – Duties of Commander-in-Chief|work=[[Hansard|Parliamentary Debates (Hansard)]]|date=4 March 1901|access-date=26 February 2012|archive-date=23 December 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121223141030/http://hansard.millbanksystems.com/lords/1901/mar/04/war-office-administration-duties-of#S4V0090P0_19010304_HOL_56|url-status=live}} Lord Wolseley was [[Gold Stick and Silver Stick|Gold Stick in Waiting]] to Queen Victoria and took part in the funeral procession following her death in February 1901.{{London Gazette|issue=27316 |supp=1|page=3552|date=22 May 1901|nolink=y}} He also served as Gold Stick in Waiting to [[Edward VII|King Edward]] during his [[Coronation of King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra|coronation]] in August 1902.{{Cite newspaper The Times |title=The Coronation |date=31 July 1902 |page=8 |issue=36834}} ===Honorific, royal appointments and arms=== In early 1901, Lord Wolseley was appointed by King [[Edward VII]] to lead a special diplomatic mission to announce the King's accession to the governments of [[Austria-Hungary]], [[Kingdom of Romania|Romania]], [[Kingdom of Serbia|Serbia]], the [[Ottoman Empire]] and [[Kingdom of Greece (Glücksburg)|Greece]].{{Cite newspaper The Times |title=The King – the special Embassies |date=23 March 1901 |page=12 |issue=36410}} During his visit to [[Constantinople]], Sultan [[Abdul Hamid II]] presented him with the [[Order of Osmanieh]] set in brilliants.{{Cite newspaper The Times |title=The King´s accession |date=12 April 1901 |page=3 |issue=36427}} He was among the original recipients of the [[Order of Merit]] in the [[1902 Coronation Honours]] list published on 26 June 1902,{{Cite newspaper The Times |title=The Coronation Honours |date=26 June 1902 |page=5 |issue=36804}} and received the order from King Edward VII at [[Buckingham Palace]] on 8 August 1902.{{Cite newspaper The Times |title=Court Circular |date=9 August 1902 |page=6 |issue=36842}}{{London Gazette|issue=27470|page=5679|date=2 September 1902| |nolink=y}} For time spent as an honorary colonel in the [[Volunteer Force (Great Britain)|Volunteer Force]], he was given the [[Volunteer Decoration|Volunteer Officers' Decoration]] on 11 August 1903.{{London Gazette|issue=27586|page=5078|date=11 August 1903|nolink=y}} He was also honorary colonel of the 23rd [[Middlesex Regiment]] from 12 May 1883,{{London Gazette|issue=25229|page=2500|date=11 May 1883|nolink=y}} honorary colonel of the Queen's Rifle Volunteer Brigade, the [[Royal Scots]] (Lothian Regiment) from 24 April 1889,{{London Gazette|issue=25926|page=2294|date=23 April 1889|nolink=y}} colonel of the [[Royal Horse Guards]] from 29 March 1895{{London Gazette|issue=26624|page=2774|date=14 May 1895|nolink=y}} and colonel-in-chief of the [[Royal Irish Regiment (1684–1922)|Royal Irish Regiment]] from 20 July 1898.{{London Gazette|issue=26988|page=4354|date=19 July 1898|nolink=y}} In retirement, he was a member of the council of the [[Union-Castle Steamship Line|Union-Castle Steamship Company]].{{Cite newspaper The Times |title=New Castle liner Walmer Castle |date=15 March 1902 |page=11 |issue=36716}} {{Infobox COA wide |image={{center|[[File:Coronet of a British Viscount.svg|150px]] [[File:Arms of Wolseley, Viscount Wolseley.svg|180px]]}} |escutcheon = Argent, a talbot {{lang|la|[[Homo homini lupus]]}}{{cite book |title=A genealogical and heraldic dictionary of the peerage and baronetage, the Privy Council, knightage and companionage |date=1915 |publisher=Harrison & Sons |location=London |page=1905 |url=https://archive.org/details/b31363945/page/1904/mode/2up?q=Wolseley |access-date=27 September 2024}} |symbolism = |notes = | previous_versions = }} ==Channel Tunnel== [[File:LionCannotFaceTheCrowingOfCock.png|thumb|left|Wolseley in a political cartoon c. 1885]] Wolseley was deeply opposed to [[Edward Watkin|Sir Edward Watkin]]'s attempt to build a [[Channel Tunnel]]. He gave evidence to a parliamentary commission that the construction might be "calamitous for England", he added that "No matter what fortifications and defences were built, there would always be the peril of some continental army seizing the tunnel exit by surprise." Various contrivances to satisfy his objections were put forward including looping the line on a viaduct from the [[White Cliffs of Dover|Cliffs of Dover]] and back into them, so that the connection could be bombarded at will by the [[Royal Navy]]. For a combination of reasons over 100 years were to pass before a permanent link was made.{{cite web|url=https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/lords/1929/jan/24/proposed-channel-tunnel|title=Proposed Channel Tunnel|work=[[Hansard|Parliamentary Debates (Hansard)]]|date=24 January 1929|access-date=25 February 2012|archive-date=18 October 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121018082236/http://hansard.millbanksystems.com/lords/1929/jan/24/proposed-channel-tunnel|url-status=live}} ==Personal life and death== [[File:Ex-libris - Garnet Wolseley, 1st Viscount Wolseley.jpg|thumb|left|''Ex libris'' with his coat of arms]] Wolseley was married in 1867 to Louisa (1843–1920), the daughter of Mr. A. Erskine.{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=311}} His only child, [[Frances Garnet Wolseley, 2nd Viscountess Wolseley|Frances]] (1872–1936) was an author and founded the College for Lady Gardeners at [[Glynde]]. She was [[Beneficiary|heiress]] to the viscountcy under special remainder, but it became extinct after her death.{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=314}} In his later years, Lord and Lady Wolseley lived in a [[grace-and-favour]] apartment at [[Hampton Court Palace]]. He and his wife were wintering at Villa Tourrette, [[Menton]] on the [[French Riviera]], where he fell ill with influenza and returned to England, where he died on 26 March 1913. He was buried on 31 March 1913 in the crypt of [[St Paul's Cathedral]], to music played by the band of the 2nd Battalion [[Royal Irish Regiment (1684–1922)|Royal Irish Regiment]], of which he was the first [[Colonel-in-Chief]].{{sfn|Heathcote|1999|p=314}}{{sfn|Geoghegan |1911}} ==Legacy== [[File:Wolseley statue, Horse Guards Parade.jpg|thumb|right|[[Equestrian statue of the Viscount Wolseley|Equestrian statue of Field Marshal Lord Wolseley]] by Goscombe John, [[Horse Guards Parade]] (2008)]] There is an [[Equestrian statue of the Viscount Wolseley|equestrian statue of Wolseley]] in [[Horse Guards Parade]] in London. This was sculpted by [[Goscombe John|Sir William Goscombe John R.A.]]{{sfn|Baker|2008|p=18}} and erected in 1920.{{cite web | url=http://www.secret-london.co.uk/Horse_Guards.html | title=Horse Guards Parade | publisher=Secret London | access-date=29 March 2013}} [[Wolseley Barracks]], at [[London, Ontario]], is a Canadian [[military base]] (now officially known as [[CFB London|ASU London]]), established in 1886. It is on the site of Wolseley Hall, the first building constructed by a [[Canadian Government]] specifically to house an element of the newly created [[Permanent Active Militia|Permanent Force]]. Wolseley Barracks has been continuously occupied by the [[Canadian Army]] since its creation, and has always housed some element of [[The Royal Canadian Regiment]]. At present, Wolseley Hall is occupied by the [[Royal Canadian Regiment Museum]] and the regiment's 4th Battalion, among other tenants.{{CRHP|14341|Wolseley Barracks|29 July 2011}} The white [[pith helmet]] worn as part of the full-dress uniform of the RCR and many other Canadian regiments is known as a Wolseley helmet.{{sfn|Bates|Suciu|2009|p=}} Wolseley is also a [[House system|senior boys house]] at the [[Duke of York's Royal Military School]].{{cite web |url=http://www.doyrms.com/structure.html |title=Structure |publisher=Duke of York's Royal Military School |access-date=25 February 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130819061447/http://www.doyrms.com/structure.html |archive-date=19 August 2013}} [[File:Colwich, Staffordshire - St Michael and All Angels Church - Lord Wolseley memorial.JPG|thumb|left|Lord Wolseley memorial at St Michael and All Angels Church in [[Colwich, Staffordshire]]]] Field Marshal Lord Wolseley is commemorated by a tablet at St Michael and All Angels Church in [[Colwich, Staffordshire]], a short distance from [[Shugborough Hall]] and Wolseley Park at Colwich, near [[Rugeley]]. The church was the burial place of the [[Wolseley baronets]] of Wolseley Park, the ancestral home of the Wolseley family.{{cite web|url=http://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/en-443128-parish-church-of-st-michael-and-all-ange|title=Parish Church of St Michael and All Angels, Colwich|publisher=British Listed Buildings|access-date=1 October 2012}} [[W. S. Gilbert]], of the musical partnership [[Gilbert and Sullivan]], may have modelled the character of Major-General Stanley in the [[operetta]] ''[[The Pirates of Penzance]]'' on Wolseley, and [[George Grossmith]], the actor who first created the role in the opening theatrical run, imitated Wolseley's appearance.{{sfn|Bradley|2005|p=220}} In another of Gilbert and Sullivan's operettas, ''[[Patience (opera)|Patience]]'', Colonel Calverley praises Wolseley in the phrase: "Skill of Sir Garnet in thrashing a cannibal".{{cite web|url=http://diamond.boisestate.edu/gas/patience/webop/pat03.html|title=Patience Web Opera|work=diamond.boisestate.edu|access-date=17 April 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303193410/http://diamond.boisestate.edu/gas/patience/webop/pat03.html|archive-date=3 March 2016|url-status=dead}} [[File:Sir Garnet pub 1883 drawing.jpg|thumb|The Sir Garnet pub in 1883]] The residential areas of [[Wolseley, Winnipeg|Wolseley]] in [[Winnipeg, Manitoba]], Canada, located in the west central part of the city{{cite web|url=http://www.mhs.mb.ca/docs/features/walkingtours/wolseley/index.shtml |title=An Historical Walking Tour of Wolseley (Winnipeg)|publisher=The Manitoba Historical Society|access-date=25 February 2012}} and of [[Wolseley, Saskatchewan]], Canada, are named after him.{{cite web|url=http://www.dunncanada.com/harrowsmith.shtml|title=Wolseley: My Kind of Town|publisher=Harrowsmith Country Life|date=April 2000|access-date=25 February 2012|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120220160149/http://www.dunncanada.com/harrowsmith.shtml|archive-date=20 February 2012}} The town of [[Wolseley, Western Cape]], South Africa, is named after Sir Garnet Joseph Wolseley. It was established on the farm Goedgevonden in 1875 and attained municipal status in 1955; prior to this it was known as Ceres Road.{{sfn|Raper|1989|p=479}} The Sir Garnet pub in the centre of [[Norwich]], overlooking the historic market place and city hall, is named after Field Marshal Lord Wolseley. The pub opened in about 1861 and adopted the name Sir Garnet Wolseley in 1874, changed after a brief closing (2011–2012) to Sir Garnet.{{cite web |url=http://www.vintagenorwich.co.uk/2012/05/a-new-life-for-sir-garnet/ |title=A New Life for Sir Garnet |author=Gemma |date=30 May 2012 |work=Vintage Norwich |access-date=2 May 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140502232346/http://www.vintagenorwich.co.uk/2012/05/a-new-life-for-sir-garnet/ |archive-date=2 May 2014 |url-status=dead}}{{cite web |url=http://www.norwich-market.org.uk/Pubs/sir_garnet_wolseley.shtm |title=Sir Garnet Wolseley |work=Norwich Market |publisher=Norwich Heritage Projects |access-date=2 May 2014}}{{cite web |url=http://www.thesirgarnet.co.uk/about/ |title=About the Sir Garnet |publisher=The Sir Garnet |access-date=2 May 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140503022510/http://www.thesirgarnet.co.uk/about/ |archive-date=3 May 2014}}{{cite news |url=http://www.eveningnews24.co.uk/news/norwich_market_place_to_get_the_sir_garnet_wolseley_pub_back_but_with_a_different_name_1_1425314 |title=Norwich market place to get the Sir Garnet Wolseley pub back – but with a different name |author=Bale, David |work=Norwich Evening News |date=29 June 2012 |access-date=29 March 2013 |archive-date=1 July 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120701223316/http://www.eveningnews24.co.uk/news/norwich_market_place_to_get_the_sir_garnet_wolseley_pub_back_but_with_a_different_name_1_1425314 |url-status=dead }} Wolseley's uniforms, field marshal's baton and souvenirs from his various campaigns are held in the collections of the [[Glenbow Museum]] in Calgary, Alberta, Canada. Wolseley maintained a deep interest in notable individuals in early modern European history, and collected items related to many of them (for example, a box from [[Sir Francis Drake]], a watch related to [[Oliver Cromwell]], a funerary badge for [[Admiral Horatio Nelson]] and General [[James Wolfe]]'s snuff box). These are also held in the collection.{{cite web |url=http://www.glenbow.org/collections/museum/military/famous.cfm |title=Famous People & Battles |publisher=Glenbow |date=n.d. |access-date=22 May 2017 |archive-date=23 January 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190123005309/https://www.glenbow.org/collections/museum/military/famous.cfm |url-status=dead }} In recognition of his success, an expression arose: "'''all Sir Garnet'''" meaning; that everything is in good order.{{sfn|Partridge|2006|p=14}}{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2011/jul/18/army-cut-not-all-sir-garnet-editorial |title=Army cuts: Not 'All Sir Garnet' |date=18 July 2011 |newspaper=The Guardian |quote=The Victorian byword for a smart operation of any kind was 'All Sir Garnet'...|access-date=18 February 2013}} ==Selected publications by Viscount Wolseley== {{refbegin}} *{{cite book|title=The Story of a Soldier's Life|volume=I|year=1903|first=Garnet |last=Wolseley|display-authors=0|url=https://archive.org/details/storysoldierslif01wols/page/n8|publisher=Charles Scribner's Sons|location= New York}} *{{cite book|title=The Story of a Soldier's Life|volume=II|year=1904|first=Garnet |last=Wolseley|display-authors=0|url=https://archive.org/details/storyofsoldiersl02wols/page/n8|publisher=Charles Scribner's Sons|location= New York}} *{{cite journal|title=General Lee|journal=Macmillan's Magazine|date=March 1887|volume=55|issue=329|pages=321–331|url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=njp.32101038084586;view=1up;seq=173}} *{{cite book|title=Narrative of the war with China in 1860 |year= 1862|url =https://archive.org/details/narrativewarwit01wolsgoog/page/n13|publisher=Longman, Green|last=Wolseley|first=Garnet|display-authors=0}} *{{cite book|title=The soldier's pocket-book of field service|year=1874|publisher=Macmillan and Co. |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/008592397}} *{{cite book|title=The life of John Churchill, Duke of Marlborough, to the accession of Queen Anne|year=1894|publisher=R. Field Marshal Garnet Joseph Wolseley, 1st Viscount Wolseley (4 June 1833 – 25 March 1913) was an Anglo-Irish officer in the British Army. He became one of the most influential British generals after a series of victories in Canada, West Africa and Egypt, followed by a central role in modernizing the British Army in promoting efficiency.
Wolseley is considered to be one of the most prominent and decorated war heroes of the British Empire during the era of New Imperialism. He served in Burma, the Crimean War, the Indian Mutiny, China, Canada and widely throughout Africa—including his Ashanti campaign (1873–1874) and the Nile Expedition against Mahdist Sudan in 1884–85. Wolseley served as Commander-in-Chief of the Forces from 1895 to 1900. His reputation for efficiency led to the late 19th century English phrase "everything's all Sir Garnet", meaning, "All is in order."
